briefs.dtap:
Childhood Vaccine Schedule and Contraindications

contraindication, precaution or neither for DTaP (diphtheria and tetanus toxoids and acellular pertussis) · which vaccines a well infant's age allows at this visitHas the vaccine's age window opened, or closed, and can you name the criterion that makes this child ineligible?

Contraindication or notInfant visitsPractice
Bottom line

Two checks at every vaccine visit: has the child's age opened the vaccine's window, and has the window closed? Then vaccinate unless you can name the criterion that makes this child ineligible; a history that only sounds disqualifying is not one.

  • Contraindication: never give. For DTaP: anaphylaxis after a previous dose or to a component; or encephalopathy (coma, decreased consciousness, prolonged seizures) within 7 days of a previous dose with no other cause. Encephalopathy is a contraindication to pertussis vaccine only, so finish the series with DT (diphtheria and tetanus toxoids).
  • Precaution: weigh risk against benefit. In general defer; vaccination may be indicated when the benefit outweighs the risk, as in an outbreak.
  • Neither: vaccinate today.
  • Up to date at 4 months: the 2-month doses were given, so the second doses are due: DTaP, Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b), PCV (pneumococcal conjugate vaccine), IPV (inactivated poliovirus vaccine) and oral rotavirus.
Contraindication, precaution or neither
DTaP: contraindications, precautions and histories that are neither
CategoryHistories
Contraindication
(every pertussis-containing vaccine)		Anaphylaxis after a previous dose or to a component · Encephalopathy within 7 days of a previous dose, not due to another cause: give DT instead
Precaution
(defer or weigh)		Progressive or unstable neurologic disorder: infantile spasms, uncontrolled epilepsy, progressive encephalopathy; defer until neurologic status is clarified and stable · Guillain-Barré syndrome within 6 weeks of a previous tetanus-toxoid dose · Arthus-type reaction to a previous diphtheria- or tetanus-toxoid dose; defer until at least 10 years after the last tetanus-toxoid dose · Moderate or severe acute illness, with or without fever
NeitherAfter a previous dose: fever of 40.5 °C or higher within 48 hours, a hypotonic-hyporesponsive episode (collapse or shock-like state) within 48 hours, a seizure within 3 days, or inconsolable crying for 3 hours or more within 48 hours · Family history of seizures or epilepsy · Stable or resolved neurologic conditions · Personal febrile seizure · Mild illness · Recent exposure
Older sources differ Older sources, including the earlier version of this brief, list those four post-dose reactions as precautions. The CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) now lists them as conditions incorrectly perceived as contraindications or precautions.
Vaccines at the infant visits
Vaccines due at each infant visit
VisitVaccines dueAge limit that matters
2 monthsDTaP, Hib, PCV, IPV and rotavirus, first doses; hepatitis B second dose if not given at 1 monthRotavirus must start by 14 weeks 6 days
4 monthsDTaP, Hib, PCV, IPV and rotavirus, second dosesToo young for influenza (6 months) and for MMR and varicella (12 months)
6 monthsDTaP and PCV third doses; Hib third dose except with PedvaxHIB; rotavirus third dose with RV5 only; IPV and hepatitis B third doses (due 6 to 18 months); influenza in seasonRotavirus series ends by 8 months 0 days; the first influenza season needs 2 doses
12 to 15 monthsMMR and varicella first doses; hepatitis A first of 2 doses (12 to 23 months); PCV fourth dose; Hib boosterRoutine MMR and varicella start at 12 months
Schedule status, October 2026 In January 2026 the CDC moved childhood rotavirus and influenza vaccines from routine to shared clinical decision-making. A federal court stayed that change in March 2026, and the stay is under appeal. The schedule CDC now posts is the 2025 schedule, which lists both vaccines as routine; check the CDC site for the current schedule. The AAP (American Academy of Pediatrics) publishes its own schedule and opposed the change, and the NBME item keys rotavirus as a routine 4-month vaccine.
Practice
  1. 2-month-old boy is at the well-child visit for his first vaccines His father has epilepsy, and an older sister had seizures with fever His mother asks to skip the pertussis vaccine development and examination normal T 36.9 °C · HR 140/min → Neither → a family history of seizures or epilepsy is neither a contraindication nor a precaution: vaccinate today. The mother's request is a matter for counseling; it does not change the classification
  2. 6-month-old boy is brought for his third DTaP dose Two days after his 4-month dose he was hard to arouse and had a prolonged seizure Evaluation found no other cause T 36.8 °C · HR 128/min alert and interactive today → Contraindication → decreased consciousness and a prolonged seizure within 7 days of a previous dose, with no other cause, is the encephalopathy that contraindicates every pertussis-containing vaccine: complete the series with DT. A precaution is weighed; this is not
  3. 17-week-old boy is starting his infant vaccines today His family moved from another state He received only the hepatitis B birth dose growth and examination normal T 36.9 °C · HR 138/min → Rotavirus vaccine → the rotavirus series cannot start on or after 15 weeks 0 days (first dose by 14 weeks 6 days), so it is never given to him. DTaP and the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine are 2-month vaccines he is due for
  4. 4-month-old girl is due for her 4-month vaccines Runny nose and mild cough for 2 days; feeding well playful; clear nasal discharge; lungs clear T 38.1 °C · HR 150/min · respirations 40/min → Neither → a mild acute illness, with or without fever, is neither: vaccinate today. Moderate or severe acute illness is the precaution
  5. 6-month-old girl is brought for her third DTaP dose Clusters of sudden flexion spasms began 3 weeks ago and continue daily despite treatment She has lost the ability to roll over T 36.8 °C · HR 122/min → Precaution → infantile spasms are a progressive neurologic disorder: a precaution, so defer DTaP until neurologic status is clarified and stable. A brief seizure within 3 days of a dose, or a stable neurologic condition, would be neither
  6. 7-month-old girl is at a well-child visit in November Up to date on her infant vaccines She has never received influenza vaccine growth and examination normal T 36.8 °C · HR 130/min → Influenza vaccine today and a second dose in 4 weeks → influenza vaccine starts at 6 months, every season; a child aged 6 months to 8 years with fewer than 2 earlier doses, or an unknown history, gets 2 doses at least 4 weeks apart. Waiting for the 12-month visit misses this season
  7. 6-month-old girl is brought for her third DTaP dose The night after her 4-month dose her temperature reached 41 °C; it resolved within a day No seizure; well since then T 36.7 °C · HR 125/min → Neither → fever of 40.5 °C or higher within 48 hours of a previous dose is listed by the CDC as a condition incorrectly perceived as a contraindication or precaution: vaccinate today. Older sources called it a precaution
  8. 4-month-old girl is brought for her second DTaP dose Within 10 minutes of her 2-month dose she developed hives, wheezing and low blood pressure She received epinephrine in the clinic T 37.0 °C · HR 132/min → Contraindication → hives, wheezing and hypotension within minutes of a dose is anaphylaxis: a severe allergic reaction after a previous dose or to a vaccine component contraindicates that vaccine
  9. 12-month-old boy is at a well-child visit Up to date on his vaccines, including the rotavirus series Healthy, with normal growth and development examination normal; no immune problems T 36.7 °C · HR 118/min → Measles-mumps-rubella and varicella → MMR and varicella are the live injected vaccines first given at 12 to 15 months, with second doses at 4 to 6 years; the rotavirus series ended by 8 months 0 days
  10. 4-month-old girl is brought for her second DTaP dose Six hours after her 2-month dose she had a brief seizure that stopped on its own Since then she has been well, with normal development T 37.0 °C · HR 135/min → Neither → a seizure within 3 days of a previous dose is listed by the CDC as a condition incorrectly perceived as a contraindication or precaution: vaccinate today. Older sources called it a precaution. Uncontrolled seizures or a progressive neurologic disorder would be the precaution
  11. 4-month-old boy is due for his 4-month vaccines Admitted yesterday with pneumonia; needs supplemental oxygen tachypneic with right-sided crackles T 39.2 °C · HR 170/min · oxygen saturation 91% on room air → Precaution → a moderate or severe acute illness, with or without fever, is a precaution: in general defer until he recovers. A mild illness, such as a cold with low fever, is neither
How NBME framed it: question 1

4-month-old girl at a well-child visit in October Uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery; vaccines up to date Normal growth and development for age vital signs normal normal examination

Immunization against which disease is most appropriate at this time?

Competing answers
  • Chickenpox: a routine live childhood vaccine; but the first varicella dose is not given until 12 months.
  • Measles-mumps-rubella: routine and live, like rotavirus; but the first dose is at 12 months.
  • Shingles: the same virus as chickenpox; but zoster vaccine is for adults from age 50; the NBME explanation, an older source, says 60.

Down to two: rotavirus or influenza. Rotavirus: up to date at 4 months means the 2-month doses were given, so the second doses are due, rotavirus among them. The October date is a seasonal cue for influenza, but at 4 months she is below its 6-month age limit. The options form an age ladder, from rotavirus at 2 months through MMR and varicella at 12 months to zoster at 50.

Not a reason to withhold routine childhood vaccines Mild illness, with or without fever · current antibiotic therapy · preterm birth: vaccinate at chronological age, full dose (hepatitis B vaccine is an exception in certain circumstances: deferred under 2,000 g if the mother is documented to be hepatitis B surface antigen negative) · breastfeeding · family history of allergies; family history of seizures or a vaccine reaction (for DTaP) · recent exposure to an infectious disease · penicillin allergy · egg allergy: any influenza vaccine appropriate for age · pregnancy or immunosuppression in a household contact; a caregiver of a severely immunosuppressed person in a protective environment should not get LAIV (live attenuated influenza vaccine); smallpox vaccine is the exception: close household contacts are screened for its contraindications · mild local reaction (redness or swelling at the injection site) to a previous dose.
Which childhood vaccines are live
ClassVaccines
Live attenuatedRotavirus · measles · mumps · rubella · varicella; also LAIV, BCG (bacille Calmette-Guérin), oral polio and live zoster vaccine (no longer available in the United States since 2020)
Inactivated (killed)Polio · hepatitis A · injectable influenza
ToxoidDiphtheria · tetanus
Subunit or conjugateHepatitis B · pertussis · Hib · pneumococcal · meningococcal · HPV (human papillomavirus)
Schedule and timing DTaP at 2, 4 and 6 months, 15 to 18 months and 4 to 6 years · Tdap (tetanus, diphtheria and acellular pertussis booster) at 11 to 12 years and in every pregnancy, preferably early in weeks 27 to 36 · pertussis postexposure prophylaxis for household contacts within 21 days of the index patient's cough onset · live injected or nasal vaccines on the same day or at least 4 weeks apart · after IVIG (intravenous immune globulin) or blood products, defer MMR and varicella 3 to 11 months, by product.
Rotavirus and zoster Rotavirus vaccine is live and oral: do not give it with SCID (severe combined immunodeficiency) or after an intussusception. Recombinant zoster vaccine is 2 doses 2 to 6 months apart from age 50, or from age 19 with immunocompromise; older sources, including the NBME explanation, start zoster vaccine at 60.
Pairs with Aquifer Adolescent Vaccines covers the 11 to 12 year visit and influenza timing by season. Ask: has this child reached the vaccine's age window, and has the window closed?
Transferable rule

Check the child's age against each vaccine's age window before the season or the disease; a vaccine whose window has not opened, or has closed, is not given at this visit. Then vaccinate unless you can name the criterion that makes the child ineligible.
